proposer.rationale:
## Hypothesis
The parent is *unconditionally* session-sticky, so a hot session pins all its traffic to one replica. Under Mooncake's bursty arrivals with ~7k-token prompts, that replica's `pending_prefill_tokens` and in-flight count pile up while other replicas idle, which is exactly what blows up the **TTFT P99** (1.44–1.49×) and drags E2E. Cache affinity is already fully reflected in `request.cached_prefix_tokens` (the simulator refreshes it), so stickiness does not need to be a hard rule — it emerges naturally when a replica genuinely holds the prefix. The right policy is a *token-aware least-loaded + cache-aware* score: minimise the incoming uncached prefill work added to each replica's pending prefill queue, weight in-flight requests (decode/KV pressure), and softly penalise replicas near KV exhaustion (which triggers eviction/preemption tails). This adapts: it stays cache-affine when the sticky replica is also the least backlogged, and spreads away when it isn't.

proposer.rationale:
## Hypothesis

The parent blows up only on the heavy Tool workload, and it does so on **TTFT** (78s vs 32s) while TPOT stays at parity — so the failure is queueing/imbalance on the prefill side, not decode. Two design flaws explain it: (1) `1500 * outstanding_requests` is large enough relative to queued prefill that at high load the router degenerates into "least-outstanding" and abandons prefix-cache hits, which *inflates* total prefill work and creates the very queues it is trying to avoid; and (2) the KV term is a hard cliff (`max(0, kv-0.75)`) that is zero for most replicas, so KV is never equalised and replicas drift toward the 122k cap where preemption storms destroy TTFT. My fix keeps the cache-aware structure but (a) cuts the per-outstanding weight so real prefill work dominates, (b) replaces the cliff with a smooth, always-on penalty on the KV occupancy *after* this request (`kv_usage + uncached/capacity`), which both equalises memory and makes long uncached prompts avoid nearly-full replicas, and (c) retains a small session-affinity bonus so warm prefixes are not thrown away under mild contention.

## Hypothesis

The parent's hard session stickiness is what protects E2E (it never re-prefills a warm prefix), but it is also what blows up the TTFT tail: when a session's sticky replica accumulates a long prefill queue, every subsequent request of that session waits behind it. The right policy is a *soft* stickiness: keep the affinity term that makes a warm replica attractive, but add an explicit sticky bonus so we only escape to a colder replica when the queue imbalance clearly exceeds the cost of re-prefilling. For new sessions there is no affinity, so the same score naturally degrades into a cache-aware load balancer (better than the parent's pure `outstanding_requests` LOR, because it also exploits shared-prefix hits).

## Hypothesis

The parent reproduces sticky-LOR exactly: existing sessions always return home (good for cache), but **new sessions are routed by `outstanding_requests` alone**, which is a lagging, coarse load proxy. Long prompts (~7k tokens) mean a replica can have zero outstanding requests yet tens of thousands of tokens of *pending prefill*, so the parent keeps dumping new sessions onto a replica whose prefill queue is already exploding. Session stickiness then emerges naturally (the home replica scores ~0 uncached), reinforced by a modest explicit affinity discount so we don't thrash, but a genuinely backed-up home is escaped. Because `choose()` refreshes views after every assignment, the backlog term rises as a burst is spread, preventing the pile-up the parent created.

## Hypothesis

The parent is a strong **sticky-LOR** router: keeping a session pinned to its home replica maximises prefix-cache reuse, which is why its TTFT-P99 ratios (0.63–0.99) beat every heuristic. ## Hypothesis

The two inspiration policies both under-perform because they penalise exactly the thing that makes this workload cheap: a **full KV cache** is the signature of a *warm, cache-rich* replica, yet `KV_PENALTY * kv_usage` (4096 in one, `KV_MAX=25000` quadratic in the other) drives traffic *away* from those replicas toward cold ones, forcing full ~7k-token prefills. Combined with a large per-`outstanding_request` weight (400–1024), this makes the router abandon sessions on small queue differences, destroying prefix reuse and actually *increasing* total prefill work — which is why they score worse than plain sticky-LOR even though they balance load. Meanwhile the parent is *too* sticky: a continuing session never leaves a jammed replica, so its prompt rides a long prefill queue and P99 TTFT blows up (ratios 1.44–1.49).

So the fix is a middle ground: keep affinity **intrinsic** in the cost via the uncached-prefill term, but give it a **loss-aversion margin** (extra prefill is weighted above one token-equivalent, so a session migrates only when the load difference clearly exceeds the recompute it causes); price `running` decodes ~4× `waiting` requests, because running sequences drain the per-step token budget that chunked prefill needs; and never penalise ordinary warm-cache occupancy — only true KV *overflow* that would trigger preemption.

## Hypothesis

The parent's **structure** is right — a $1.5\times$ cache margin correctly prices the value of a prefix-cache hit, and its cost is dominated by `pending_prefill_tokens`. What is wrong is the **scale of the load terms**: `RUN_COST=256` / `WAIT_COST=64` are tiny next to prefill tokens (median prompt ≈ 7k). Concretely, with a full 7k-token cache hit on the home replica versus 0 elsewhere, the parent only sheds home once it has **~42 more running sequences** than the alternative — so decode batches pile up and the TPOT tail (P99 ≈ 1.09–1.12× best heuristic in the feedback) blows out. Raising `RUN_COST`/`WAIT_COST` to token-equivalent magnitudes (~1500/400, i.e. one running sequence ≈ the work of ~1.5k prefill tokens) makes the shed threshold ~7–8 extra running sequences, while keeping the cache trade-off identical. The policy then adapts automatically: under light load (few running) cache affinity dominates; under heavy load (large running counts) balance dominates. A smooth KV penalty plus the existing hard overflow wall prevents preemption storms.

## Hypothesis

The parent's biggest self-inflicted wound is **double-counting decode**: it adds `W_RUN * running` into the same `load` that drives the *shedding* decision, while `outstanding_requests` (which already includes running sequences) is counted at `W_OUT`. That inflates the home's load mostly when it is decode-heavy, so the escape hatch fires too eagerly and breaks prefix affinity — which is exactly where the parent's TTFT/E2E wins come from. Inspiration 1 (which drops that term and raises `RUN_FACTOR`) confirms this: same shedding thresholds, less spurious shedding, higher fitness. Inspiration 2 shows the opposite failure mode — piling decode penalties into *placement* plus aggressive shedding costs a lot. So the fix is to keep decode pressure out of the load used for affinity, let the `running`-based escape hatch be the *only* decode brake, and add a narrow KV-saturation escape (a home near capacity is unambiguously bad for the TPOT tail regardless of its queued load). Placement keeps a *small* running term so brand-new sessions don't land on a decode-hot replica.

## Hypothesis

The parent's shed test is effectively **dead code**: after it flags an overloaded or decode‑hot home, it re-runs the *same* cost function, which still contains the home's large cached‑prefix credit. I therefore (1) give a flagged home a `SHED_BIAS` so it is actually abandoned unless it is still clearly cheapest, and (2) add a prefill×decode interference term to the placement cost. Everything else (sticky default, shed thresholds, KV guard, relative decode penalty) is kept, since raising the decode penalty alone was shown to hurt.

## Hypothesis

The parent's TPOT tail is set by the single replica with the largest pending-prefill backlog, because chunked prefill steals decode cycles. The parent tried to cap this with a thresholded convex penalty, but two flaws blunt it:

1. **Wrong reference level.** The convex penalty and the `prefill_hot` shed test both use the cluster *mean* pending prefill. The hot replica itself drags that mean upward, so the test "home > 1.5·avg + 1500" rarely fires when the home is the outlier — exactly the case we want to shed.

Fix: keep sticky affinity (it is what wins E2E/TTFT), but (a) reference pending prefill against the cluster **minimum** rather than the mean, so a hot home is detected even when it is the one inflating the mean, and (b) lower the convex margin and strengthen the coefficient so a modestly hot backlog is already priced. Use the **median** running batch (robust to the hot outlier) as the decode reference, as Inspiration 1 showed. When all replicas are equally loaded, min≈median≈mean, so equal-load placements still don't spread and cache affinity is preserved.
